mainTopic: The end of the wine-sale case, a lender living in the borrower's courtyard as רבית, and a lender using his debtors' slaves
overview: This amud opens by finishing an earlier case about a wine sale. That deal is attacked as קרוב לשכר ורחוק להפסד, likely gain with little risk, which is rabbinic רבית. אביי answers that the buyer also risks a drop in price, so the deal could go either way and is allowed. Next, a new משנה teaches that a lender may not live in the borrower's courtyard for free or at cheap rent, because that is רבית. רב נחמן adds that the lender must pay rent even in a case where a squatter would owe nothing. The גמרא shows this goes beyond the משנה: it covers a courtyard that is never rented out and a lender who has somewhere else to live. A second version limits רב נחמן's rule to a borrower who said 'lend me and live in my courtyard.' Last, רבא questions his father, רב יוסף בר חמא, for working his debtors' slaves. His father first relies on רב נחמן, then, after רבא rejects that source, on רב's ruling that one who works another's slave is exempt, a ruling that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The wine deal looks like likely gain with no real risk
steps.stepSummary: The deal from the earlier discussion is attacked as קרוב לשכר ורחוק להפסד, which is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: This deal is close to gain and far from loss.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the end of an earlier discussion about a wine sale. Someone objects that the deal is forbidden because it is set up so that one side is likely to gain and unlikely to lose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A deal that is קרוב לשכר ורחוק להפסד gives one side a likely profit with almost no risk, and that looks like רבית. The objection is that taking on the risk of the wine going sour is not enough to make the deal fair. This sets up אביי's reply in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Close to gain: profit is likely
Far from loss: there is little real risk of losing

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the start of a new topic. It is the tail end of the previous discussion about a wine sale, so it leans on details from the earlier part of the daf.

phrases.english: This is close to gain
and far from loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי קָרוֹב לְשָׂכָר וְרָחוֹק לְהֶפְסֵד הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the wine-sale discussion from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wine-sale arrangement discussed earlier on the daf
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The deal gives one side a likely profit with little risk, so it should count as rabbinic רבית.

steps.title: The buyer also takes the risk of a price drop, so the deal can go either way
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that since the buyer accepts the risk of the price falling, the deal is קרוב לזה ולזה and is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: since he accepts the risk of a price drop, it is close to this and to that.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends the deal. He points out that the buyer also takes a risk, the risk that the price will go down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection said the deal was one-sided. אביי shows it is not, because the buyer can lose if the price drops. A deal where either gain or loss is possible, קרוב לזה ולזה, is a normal business risk and is not רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: Accepts upon himself, takes the risk
Close to this and to that: gain and loss are both possible

steps.whatToRemember: A deal is forbidden as rabbinic רבית when it is קרוב לשכר ורחוק להפסד. When both gain and loss are real possibilities (קרוב לזה ולזה), it is allowed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a basic test for business deals in הלכות רבית: is the risk real for both sides, or is one side almost guaranteed a profit?

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is אביי answering the objection.

phrases.english: since he accepts upon himself a drop in price,
it is close to this and to that.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ כֵּיוָן דִּמְקַבֵּל עֲלֵיהּ זוֹלָא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a missing factor: the buyer carries a real risk too
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The deal looked like one-sided gain, which would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the buyer accepts the risk of a price drop, the deal is קרוב לזה ולזה and is allowed.

steps.title: A lender may not live in the borrower's courtyard for free or for cheap
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a lender may not live free in the borrower's courtyard or rent from him below the going rate, because that is רבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who lends to his friend may not live in his courtyard for free, and may not rent from him for less, because that is interest.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts here. It says a lender may not get free or cheap housing from the person who borrowed from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבית is not only extra money paid back. Any benefit the lender gets because of the loan, such as free or cheap housing, counts as payment for the loan. So the lender must pay full rent.

keyTerms.meaning: For less than the normal price
Interest, forbidden payment for a loan

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who lends to his friend
may not live in his courtyard for free,
and may not rent from him for less,
because it is interest.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ לֹא יָדוּר בַּחֲצֵרוֹ חִנָּם
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender may not live free or at reduced rent in the borrower's courtyard, because the benefit counts as רבית.

steps.title: רב נחמן: a lender living in the borrower's courtyard must pay rent
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן teaches that although someone living in another's courtyard without permission usually does not pay, a lender living in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: even though they said that one who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge does not need to pay him rent, if he lent him money and lives in his courtyard, he must pay rent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a statement of רב נחמן. He compares two cases: normally a squatter does not pay rent, but a lender must.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere the רבנן taught that a person who lives in someone's courtyard without asking does not owe rent, because the owner lost nothing. רב נחמן says the loan changes things: the lender's free stay would be a benefit tied to the loan, so it is רבית and he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: One who lives in his friend's courtyard

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that an act that is normally free of charge becomes forbidden רבית once a loan is in the picture.

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said
that Rav Nachman said:
Even though they said
phrases.notes: This points to a well-known rule taught in בבא קמא about living in someone's courtyard without asking.

phrases.english: one who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge
does not need to pay him rent,
if he lent him money and lives in his courtyard,
he must pay him rent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An אמורא's statement on the topic of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender who lives in the borrower's courtyard must pay rent, even though a squatter usually would not have to.

steps.title: Why say it? The משנה already teaches this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב נחמן adds, since the משנה already says a lender may not live in the borrower's courtyard for free.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned: one who lends to his friend may not live in his courtyard for free, and may not rent from him for less, because it is interest!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן. His rule seems to repeat what our משנה already says.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes that an אמורא does not just repeat a משנה. Since the משנה already forbids free housing for a lender, רב נחמן's statement looks unnecessary. This challenge sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (what is new here?)

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned: One who lends to his friend
may not live in his courtyard for free,
and may not rent from him for less,
because it is interest!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's statement as already found in the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already rules that a lender may not live free in the borrower's courtyard, so the statement seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The משנה alone might cover only a courtyard normally rented and a man who normally rents
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה alone we might limit the rule to a rentable courtyard and a person who normally rents. רב נחמן teaches that the rule applies even when neither is true.
steps.simpleTranslation: If from our משנה, I would have said: this applies only to a courtyard that stands to be rented and a man who usually rents. But a courtyard that does not stand to be rented and a man who does not usually rent, I would say no. So he teaches us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows that רב נחמן adds a case the משנה might not have covered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner never rents out the courtyard and the lender has another place to live, it seems nobody gains and nobody loses, so we might think no rent is owed. רב נחמן's comparison to the squatter case shows that even then the lender must pay. This is the very case where a squatter would owe nothing, and still the loan makes free housing into רבית.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have said (a possible but wrong first thought)
These words apply only (to this case)
I might say no (the rule does not apply)

steps.whatToRemember: A lender must pay rent for living in the borrower's courtyard even if the courtyard is never rented out and the lender has somewhere else to live. The loan alone makes free housing into רבית.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב נחמן is repeating the משנה. His new point is the case of 'no loss, no gain', where without a loan no rent would be owed.

phrases.english: If from our משנה, I would have said:
this applies only to a courtyard that stands to be rented out,
and a man who usually rents.
But a courtyard that does not stand to be rented out,
and a man who does not usually rent,
I might say no; so he teaches us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5 by showing what רב נחמן adds.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Widens the scope: the אמורא's statement covers a case the משנה might not have included
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה applies only when the courtyard is normally rented and the lender normally rents, so there is real gain and loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with a courtyard not for rent and a man who does not normally rent, the lender must pay rent because of רבית.

steps.title: Second version of רב נחמן: only when the borrower said 'lend me and live here'
steps.stepSummary: In a different version, רב נחמן says the lender must pay rent when the owner said 'Lend me money and live in my courtyard.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say it this way: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: Even though the rule is that someone who lives in another person's courtyard without permission does not need to pay rent, if the owner says 'Lend me money and live in my courtyard,' the lender must pay rent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way that רב נחמן's ruling was reported. In this version the case is narrower: the owner himself tied the loan to living in the courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version (step 4), the rule covered any lender living in his borrower's courtyard. Here the rule is tied to a case where the borrower openly said 'lend me and live in my courtyard.' That wording links the free stay directly to the loan, so it looks like רבית.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument. It is the same teaching of רב נחמן reported a different way, and the difference is only which case it covers.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said
that Rav Nachman said:
Even though they said
that one who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge
does not need to pay him rent,
if the owner says "Lend me and live in my courtyard,"
the lender must pay him rent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of רב נחמן's ruling from step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the borrower said 'lend me and live in my courtyard,' the lender must pay rent.

steps.title: How the two versions differ
steps.stepSummary: The first version forbids even a plain loan, and so it surely forbids 'lend me.' The second version forbids only 'lend me,' not a plain loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who said the rule applies when he simply lent him money, all the more so it applies when the owner said 'lend me.' According to the one who said 'lend me,' the rule applies only then, but if he simply lent him money, it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the practical difference between the two versions of רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version is stricter: even a plain loan with no mention of the courtyard requires rent, so an open 'lend me and live here' surely does. The second version is more lenient: without that open link, a plain loan does not require rent. This sets up the next question, which is why the plain loan would be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: He lent him: a plain loan with nothing said about the courtyard

phrases.english: The one who said "he lent him"
phrases.notes: This means the first version (step 4), where a plain loan is enough to require rent.

phrases.english: would say all the more so for "lend me."
And the one who said "lend me"
would say: but "he lent him," no.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר הִלְוָהוּ – כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן הַלְוֵינִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the version in step 7 with the version in step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First version: a plain loan or 'lend me' both require rent. Second version: only 'lend me' requires rent.

steps.title: Why is a plain loan allowed in the second version?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the lenient version.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why, in the second version, a lender who simply lent money may live in the courtyard for free. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain loan followed by a free stay could still look like a reward for the loan. The גמרא wants to know why that is not treated as רבית.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the lenient side of step 8
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a plain loan does not require rent according to the second version

steps.title: The loan was not given for the sake of living there
steps.stepSummary: Since the money was not lent with the stay in mind, there is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since from the start he did not lend him the money with this in mind, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that when the loan was given, nobody had the free stay in mind, so the stay is not payment for the loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבית needs a link between the loan and the benefit. Here the loan came first with no talk of the courtyard, so the free stay is not seen as interest. When the borrower says 'lend me and live here,' that link is stated openly.

keyTerms.meaning: With this in mind; for this purpose
We have no problem with it

steps.whatToRemember: According to the second version, a free stay is forbidden only when the loan was openly tied to it ('lend me and live here'). A plain loan given with no such link is allowed.

phrases.english: Since from the start
he did not lend him with this in mind,
we have no problem with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא לָאו אַדַּעְתָּא דְּהָכִי אוֹזְפֵיהּ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The loan was not given with the stay in mind, so the stay is not interest.

steps.title: רב יוסף בר חמא used his debtors' slaves
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא would seize the slaves of people who owed him money and make them work for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר חמא would seize the slaves of people who owed him money, and he would make them do work for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about a lender who benefited from his borrowers' slaves. This sets up the conversation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using a debtor's slave for free looks like getting a benefit because of the loan, much like the free courtyard stay. The next steps ask whether this is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Would seize or take hold of
Whom he was owed money by; who owed him money

phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Chama
would seize the slaves of people
who owed him money,
and he would have them do work.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא תָּקֵיף עַבְדֵי דְאִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about a lender benefiting from his borrower's property
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף בר חמא's practice: using the slaves of people who owed him money.

steps.title: רבא asks his father why he does this
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks his father what his reason is for using the slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: His son רבא said to him: What is the reason the master does this?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא questions his father's practice. The question really expresses surprise, because the practice looks like a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking someone's slave and working him seems to cause the owner a loss, and here it also looks like a benefit taken because of the loan. רבא wants the source that permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: The master: a respectful way of saying 'you'

phrases.english: Rava his son said to him:
What is the reason the master does this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא בְּרֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא עָבֵיד מָר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the practice described in step 11
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The legal basis for using a debtor's slaves for free

steps.title: Relying on רב נחמן: a slave is not worth his food
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא answers that he follows רב נחמן, who said a slave is not even worth the food he eats.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I hold like רב נחמן, for רב נחמן said: A slave is not worth the bread in his stomach.
steps.whatsHappening: The father explains that the owner loses nothing, because a slave's work is worth less than the food he gets.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the slave eats at the lender's home and his work is worth less than his food, the lender gains nothing and the owner loses nothing. So there is no theft and no real benefit from the loan.

keyTerms.meaning: I hold; this is my opinion
The bread of his belly; the food he eats

phrases.english: He said to him:
I hold like Rav Nachman,
for Rav Nachman said:
A slave is not worth the bread of his belly.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A slave's work is worth less than his food, so using him causes no loss.

steps.title: רבא: רב נחמן meant only a useless slave
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that רב נחמן said this only about a lazy slave like דארו, not about ordinary working slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You can say רב נחמן said this about someone like his slave דארו, who just dances among the barrels. Did he say it about other slaves?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back. He limits רב נחמן's saying to one useless slave, so it cannot be used for ordinary slaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary slaves do real work that is worth more than their food. So the owner does lose something, and the free work could count as a benefit from the loan. רב נחמן's saying is narrowed to a special case.

keyTerms.meaning: Say; you can say (limiting a statement)

phrases.english: He said to him:
Say that Rav Nachman said this
about someone like Daru, his slave,
phrases.notes: דארו was רב נחמן's own slave.

phrases.english: who dances among the barrels,
phrases.notes: He means a slave who fools around instead of working.

phrases.english: but did he say it about other slaves?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימוֹר דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן כְּגוֹן דָּארוּ עַבְדֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source brought in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: Using רב נחמן's saying to allow working ordinary slaves
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב נחמן spoke about a useless slave. Ordinary slaves' work is worth more than their food, so the saying does not apply to them.

steps.title: Relying on רב: one who works another's slave is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא now relies on רב, quoted by רב דניאל בר רב קטינא: one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I hold like this ruling that רב דניאל בר רב קטינא said in the name of רב: One who seizes his friend's slave and has him do work is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רבא rejected the first source, the father gives a new one. He relies on רב, who says someone who works another person's slave does not have to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This source does not depend on the slave being lazy. It applies to any slave, so it answers רבא's challenge. The statement continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt; does not have to pay

phrases.english: He said to him: I,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר רַב קַטִּינָא
phrases.english: like this ruling of Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina
that he said in the name of Rav, that is what I hold.
For he said:
One who seizes his friend's slave
and has him do work
is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא, כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר רַב קַטִּינָא אָמַר רַב סְבִירָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the source that רבא rejected in step 14 with a new source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רב, one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt, whatever the slave's value.
